solution.concept_anchor: 51A(g) — positive obligation on citizens and industries, not just State
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know 'Article 21 covers environment' will select option (a) as the right's source — but the question asks about the constitutional basis for imposing obligations on the private chemical company (a non-State actor), for which 51A(g) provides the duty-based justification used by courts.
elimination_logic: The scenario involves a private chemical company (non-State actor) causing environmental damage — the question asks what constitutional principle supports imposing obligations on it.
Eliminate (a): Article 21 is a Fundamental Right enforceable against the State — it does not directly impose obligations on private companies; it creates rights for citizens.
Eliminate (b): Article 48A is a DPSP directed at the State — it directs the government to protect the environment, not private industries directly.
Eliminate (d): Article 32 is the remedy (writ jurisdiction) for FR enforcement against the State — it is a procedural provision, not the substantive basis for industry obligations.

Confirm (c): Article 51A(g) imposes a duty on every citizen to protect the environment — courts have extended this to impose obligations on private actors and industries, especially in PIL proceedings. This is the constitutional basis for judicially imposing environmental obligations on non-State actors.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap extends Article 21's reach to cover private parties directly. While Article 21 has been the vehicle for environmental rights jurisprudence, it creates rights against the State — not direct obligations on private companies. Article 51A(g), being a citizen duty (which extends to corporate citizens and industries through judicial interpretation), provides the constitutional basis for imposing environmental obligations on non-State actors. Students who know 'Article 21 + environment' without distinguishing the right-holder versus duty-bearer will select option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
The constitutional basis for imposing environmental obligations on private industrial actors requires understanding the distinct roles of Article 21 (FR against State) and Article 51A(g) (citizen duty, judicially extended to private actors).

In this scenario, the chemical company is a private entity, not a State actor. The question is which constitutional provision supports imposing direct environmental obligations on it.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Article 21 grants citizens the right to a clean environment — it operates as a right against State action. While courts have used Article 21 to compel the State to regulate private polluters, Article 21 itself does not directly impose obligations on private companies.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Article 48A directs the State (not private entities) to protect and improve the environment — it is a governance directive, not an obligation on industrial actors.
• Option (c) — Correct: Article 51A(g) imposes a duty on 'every citizen' to protect and improve the natural environment. Courts, particularly in the MC Mehta series, have used this provision to impose positive environmental obligations on industries, municipalities, and private actors — effectively judicializing a non-justiciable duty through PIL.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Article 32 is the writ remedy for enforcing Fundamental Rights against the State — it is a procedural provision, not a substantive source of environmental obligations on private parties.

Value Addition:
• The 'polluter pays' principle, developed in MC Mehta cases, flows from 51A(g)-based judicial reasoning.
• National Green Tribunal (NGT) adjudicates environmental disputes under the NGT Act 2010 — a statutory mechanism complementing PIL-based 51A(g) enforcement.
• Constitutional morality and environmental duty now interact in cases involving indigenous land rights versus industrial development.

statement_analysis.reason: The majority (4:1) relied on constitutional morality, equality, and Article 51A(e) — the duty to renounce practices derogatory to women — as converging constitutional values that supported striking down the exclusionary practice.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(e) alone, without support from other constitutional provisions or legislative backing, can directly override a Fundamental Right established under Articles 25–26 when the two conflict.
statement_analysis.reason: FDs are non-justiciable; they cannot independently override FRs. The Sabarimala majority used 51A(e) alongside Articles 14, 15, 17, and 25 — not as a standalone override. FDs require legislative backing or conjunction with justiciable provisions to override an established FR.

statement_analysis.statement: The minority opinion in the Sabarimala case, delivered by Justice Indu Malhotra, held that constitutional morality should yield to popular morality in matters of religious denomination — dissenting from the majority's use of 51A(e) and equality.
statement_analysis.reason: Justice Indu Malhotra's dissent held the opposite — that courts should not interfere with essential religious practices of a denomination and that the question involved matters of faith beyond judicial adjudication. She did not argue that popular morality should override constitutional morality — she questioned whether this was justiciable.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students aware of the Sabarimala controversy and its five-judge composition may accept all three statements as broadly capturing the case's constitutional themes without scrutinising the precise holdings of the majority and minority.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The Sabarimala majority did use 51A(e) as a supporting value alongside equality — Statement 1 accurately describes this. Correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: '51A(e) alone...can directly override' — the word 'alone' and 'directly' are the flags. FDs are non-justiciable and cannot independently override FRs. Incorrect.

Evaluate Statement 3: Indu Malhotra J.'s dissent was about non-justiciability of essential religious practices — not about 'popular morality yielding to constitutional morality.' Statement 3 mischaracterises her reasoning. Incorrect.
Only Statement 1 is correct — select option (b): '1 only.'
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statements 2 and 3 both exploit the partial-truth technique. Statement 2 contains the true fact that 51A(e) was involved in Sabarimala but adds the false claim that it 'alone' can 'directly override' an FR. Statement 3 correctly identifies Indu Malhotra J. as the dissenter but mischaracterises her reasoning — she did not say 'popular morality should override constitutional morality'; she questioned justiciability. Students who know 'Sabarimala + dissent + Indu Malhotra' without the precise reasoning will accept Statement 3.
solution.final_explanation:
Sabarimala is a landmark case where the intersection of FDs, equality, and religious freedom was adjudicated at the highest constitutional level.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 4:1 majority used Article 51A(e) as a constitutional value supporting the striking down of the age-based exclusion of women. The majority drew on the synergy between Articles 14, 15, 17, 25, and 51A(e) to construct a constitutional morality argument.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The word 'alone' renders this false. FDs are non-justiciable — they cannot independently override FRs. In Sabarimala, 51A(e) was one strand in a multi-pronged constitutional argument, not a standalone override mechanism.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Justice Indu Malhotra's dissent held that matters of faith and essential religious practice of a denomination are not subject to judicial review in this manner — she was questioning justiciability, not arguing that popular morality should prevail over constitutional morality (she actually wrote in defence of constitutional morality in religious contexts).

Value Addition:
• The Sabarimala review petition was referred to a nine-judge Constitutional Bench — the case remains constitutionally significant.
• The case raised the critical question of what constitutes an 'essential religious practice' under Article 25.
• 51A(e) is the only FD that explicitly names women as a protected category — giving it unique relevance in gender-equality jurisprudence.

solution.concept_anchor: Verma Committee — existing laws implicitly enforce FDs

statement_analysis.statement: The Justice J.S. Verma Committee (2012) recommended that a separate and dedicated 'Fundamental Duties Enforcement Act' should be enacted as a comprehensive legislation to impose criminal penalties for every violation of each of the eleven duties listed under Article 51A.
statement_analysis.reason: The Verma Committee recommended that FDs should be made legally enforceable through legislation — but it did not recommend a single omnibus 'Fundamental Duties Enforcement Act' imposing criminal penalties for every duty. The committee noted that many existing laws already implicitly enforce FDs and recommended targeted legislative action, not a single comprehensive criminal statute.

statement_analysis.statement: The Verma Committee observed that many existing laws — such as environmental protection legislation and anti-discrimination laws — already implicitly enforce Fundamental Duties, even though Article 51A itself provides no direct enforcement mechanism.
statement_analysis.reason: This is an accurate summary of the Committee's key observation — it noted that Parliament had already enacted laws giving effect to FDs without explicitly saying so, and recommended building on this foundation rather than creating entirely new enforcement mechanisms.

statement_analysis.statement: The Verma Committee recommended that educational institutions should include Fundamental Duties in their curricula as a mandatory component, linking this to the Right to Education framework and Article 51A(k).
statement_analysis.reason: The Committee did recommend mandatory teaching of FDs in educational institutions, recognising the connection between civic education, Article 51A(k) (parental duty to educate), and the RTE framework — consistent with a citizenship-oriented approach to FD enforcement.

solution.strong_distractor: a — '1 only' is the strong distractor because Statement 1 sounds authoritative — 'Fundamental Duties Enforcement Act with criminal penalties' sounds like exactly the kind of recommendation a post-Nirbhaya law commission would make. Students may accept it without scrutinising the 'every violation' and 'criminal penalties' elements.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: A comprehensive 'Fundamental Duties Enforcement Act' with criminal penalties for every duty — this is an overstatement. The Committee recommended targeted legislation building on existing laws, not an omnibus criminal statute. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: The Committee's observation that existing laws already implicitly enforce FDs is accurately stated. Statement 2 IS correct — eliminate from 'incorrect' pool.
Evaluate Statement 3: Recommending FDs in educational curricula is accurately attributed to the Committee. Statement 3 IS correct — eliminate.
Only Statement 1 is NOT correct — select option (c): '1 only.'
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is a plausible-fabrication trap. It uses accurate elements (Verma Committee, Fundamental Duties enforcement, legislation) but fabricates the specific recommendation — an omnibus 'Fundamental Duties Enforcement Act' with criminal penalties for each duty. The Committee's actual recommendation was more nuanced: use existing legislative frameworks, fill gaps through targeted legislation, and build civic awareness. The fabricated recommendation sounds reasonable and specific enough that students who know 'Verma Committee recommended enforcement' will not scrutinise the details.
solution.final_explanation:
The Justice J.S. Verma Committee's recommendations on FDs represent a pragmatic, graduated approach to enforcement — not a sweeping criminalization.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: The Committee did not recommend a single comprehensive 'Fundamental Duties Enforcement Act' imposing criminal penalties for violating each of the eleven duties. Such an approach would face serious Article 19 and 21 challenges. The Committee's approach was to build on existing implicit enforcement mechanisms and advocate targeted legislation.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Committee's most important observation was that India already had a web of laws — environmental protection, anti-discrimination, national honour — that give effect to FDs without explicitly naming them. This observation supported a legislative gap-filling approach rather than wholesale new legislation.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Committee recommended integrating FDs into school and college curricula, recognising that civic awareness is as important as legal enforcement. This connects to Article 51A(k) and the RTE framework.

Value Addition:
• Verma Committee submitted its report in January 2013 — within 30 days of being constituted, a remarkable speed.
• The Criminal Law (Amendment) Act 2013 was passed based on the Committee's recommendations on sexual violence — the FD-related recommendations were separately noted.
• The distinction between 'moral obligation' and 'legal obligation' that the Committee sought to bridge remains an open constitutional question.

solution.concept_anchor: Bijoe Emmanuel — right not to sing upheld; duty of respect ≠ compulsion to perform
solution.strong_distractor: b — The Shyam Narayan Chouksey case also involved the national anthem in a public venue, and SC initially mandated anthem-playing — students may associate 'upholding right to not participate' with Chouksey rather than Bijoe Emmanuel.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act (1971) prohibits disrespect to national symbols — it does not 'uphold the right to remain silent during the anthem.' It creates statutory penalties, not rights.
Eliminate (b): Shyam Narayan Chouksey v. UOI resulted in a direction to play the anthem in cinema halls — the opposite of protecting non-participation rights (though later modified).
Eliminate (c): The 42nd Amendment inserted FDs including the duty to respect the anthem — it created the duty, not a right to non-participation.

Confirm (d): Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986) upheld the students' right to stand respectfully but not sing the anthem — the SC held FRs under Articles 19(1)(a) and 25 protect this refusal. This is the correctly matched pair.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap operates between Bijoe Emmanuel and Shyam Narayan Chouksey — both involve the national anthem in public settings. Students who recall 'anthem case + Supreme Court' without distinguishing the holdings may assign Chouksey the Bijoe Emmanuel holding. The distinction: Bijoe Emmanuel protected non-participation; Chouksey initially mandated participation (later modified). These are opposite outcomes from cases involving the same subject matter — a classic UPSC entity-swap scenario.
solution.final_explanation:
The national anthem cases represent a fascinating evolution in the judicial understanding of the right to symbolic expression and conscientious non-participation.

• Option (a) — Incorrectly matched: The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971, establishes criminal liability for actively insulting national symbols. It does not create or protect a right to remain silent during the anthem — it is a restriction statute, not a rights-protection ruling.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: Shyam Narayan Chouksey v. Union of India resulted in an SC direction mandating the playing of the national anthem in cinema halls — an enforcement of the duty, not a protection of the right to non-participation. The order was later modified.
• Option (c) — Incorrectly matched: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, inserted Article 51A including the duty to respect the national anthem — it codified a duty, not a right to refrain from participating.
• Option (d) — Correctly matched: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986) is the case where three Jehovah's Witnesses students stood respectfully but did not sing the anthem. The SC upheld their right under Articles 19(1)(a) and 25, holding that the Fundamental Duty to respect the anthem does not compel active vocal participation.

Value Addition:
• Bijoe Emmanuel is a seminal case on compelled speech and freedom of conscience globally.
• The case distinguished between 'respect' (standing silently) and 'active expression' (singing) — a crucial interpretive distinction.
• The Chouksey case was ultimately modified — mandatory anthem-playing in cinema halls is no longer judicially mandated.

solution.concept_anchor: 42nd Amendment — Emergency legitimacy; India's deliberate non-coercive approach to FDs
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who accept both A and R as factually true (correctly) may assume that the Emergency's authoritarian context 'explains' India's adoption of a softer, non-coercive FD model — when in fact the causal direction runs the other way: the Swaran Singh Committee's deliberate choice of the non-coercive model preceded and independently motivated the design of FDs.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — The 42nd Amendment was enacted in 1976 during the Emergency and has faced constitutional legitimacy questions, including about the political conditions under which it was passed. A is factually correct.

Step 2: Is R correct? — The Swaran Singh Committee did draw from the USSR model where rights and duties were co-equal and co-enforceable; India deliberately chose a softer, non-coercive model. R is factually correct.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — R explains the design philosophy of FDs (why they are non-coercive), not why the 42nd Amendment's Emergency-era passage raises legitimacy concerns. The legitimacy concern arises from the political context of Emergency, not from the non-coercive design philosophy. R does not explain A.

Both A and R are correct, but R does not explain A — correct option is (c)... wait. Checking: A correct, R correct, R does not explain A → option (b). Re-mapping: A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A → 'b'. Correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This is a subtle reversed-causation trap. Both A (Emergency legitimacy concerns about 42nd Amendment) and R (India's deliberate choice of non-coercive FD model) are true. The trap is assuming R explains A — that because India adopted a non-coercive model, the Amendment has legitimacy concerns. In fact, the legitimacy concern arises independently from the Emergency context (suspended rights, political opposition, extended Parliament term) — not from whether the FDs are coercive or not. R describes the design philosophy; A describes the political legitimacy concern — these are parallel facts, not causally linked.
solution.final_explanation:
The 42nd Amendment's constitutional legitimacy and India's deliberate non-coercive approach to FDs are both significant constitutional facts — but their causal relationship must be carefully analysed.

Assertion (A): Correct. The 42nd Amendment was passed during the 1975–77 Emergency when fundamental rights were suspended, political opposition was imprisoned, and Parliament's term had been extended. This context raises legitimate questions about whether amendments passed during this period reflect genuine constitutional consensus.

Reason (R): Correct. The Swaran Singh Committee studied the USSR Constitution (where rights and duties were co-equal and co-enforceable) and deliberately recommended a softer model — duties without co-equal enforceability. India's approach was a middle path, avoiding both ignoring duties (early constitutions) and making them coercive (authoritarian models).

Causal link: R does NOT explain A. The legitimacy concerns about the 42nd Amendment arise from the Emergency's political context — suspended rights, political prisoners, unrepresentative Parliament. These concerns are independent of whether the FDs adopted were coercive or non-coercive. R is a statement about constitutional design philosophy; A is about political legitimacy — they are parallel, independent facts.

Value Addition:
• Sarkaria Commission (1983) reviewed Emergency-era amendments — several were rolled back by the 43rd and 44th Amendments (1977–78).
• The 44th Amendment repealed several 42nd Amendment provisions — but FDs in Part IV-A were retained.
• India's non-coercive FD model is often contrasted with China's constitutional duties, which are enforceable alongside rights.

solution.concept_anchor: 51A(f) composite culture — pluralistic, not majoritarian; Articles 29–30 reinforce
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) about majority cultural claims using 51A(f) to override Article 29–30 minority rights sounds constitutionally reasonable — if the duty is to preserve national culture, it might seem natural that it could supersede minority cultural rights. Students who haven't read that courts have not resolved this may accept (c) as falsely 'settled' in favour of majority culture.
elimination_logic: Identify the common category: Three statements accurately describe the constitutional relationship between 51A(f) and minority cultural rights under Articles 29–30.
Option (a): 51A(f)'s 'composite culture' language being interpreted as pluralistic and inclusive is accurate — this is the prevailing judicial reading. Common category.
Option (b): Articles 29–30 are reinforced by 51A(f) because cultural preservation becomes a national duty, not just a minority privilege — accurate. Common category.
Option (d): DPSP + FDs together protecting cultural pluralism — both address cultural preservation from different directions. Accurate. Common category.

Option (c): Courts having 'definitively resolved' that majority cultural claims under 51A(f) override minority rights under Articles 29–30 — this is factually false. Courts have explicitly NOT resolved this question. Option (c) is the odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) uses the conflation technique — merging the real constitutional tension (majority vs. minority cultural claims) with a false resolution (courts definitively resolving in favour of majority claims). Students who know the Sabarimala controversy involved majority religious practice vs. minority-like protections may assume similar resolution has occurred in the cultural domain. The key fact: courts have explicitly left open whether majority cultural claims under 51A(f) can override minority rights under Articles 29–30 — no definitive judicial answer exists.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between the duty to preserve composite culture (51A(f)) and minority cultural rights (Articles 29–30) is one of harmony with an unresolved tension.

• Option (a): Accurate. The word 'composite' in 51A(f) has been consistently interpreted as requiring pluralistic, inclusive cultural preservation — not the imposition of any single cultural tradition. This reading is harmonious with Articles 29–30.
• Option (b): Accurate. Articles 29–30 are reinforced by 51A(f) because making cultural preservation a national duty elevates minority cultural rights from a group privilege to a nationally recognised constitutional value.
• Option (c) — Odd one out: Courts have NOT definitively resolved whether majority cultural claims under 51A(f) can override minority rights under Articles 29–30. This is explicitly an open constitutional question. The statement fabricates a judicial resolution that does not exist.
• Option (d): Accurate. DPSPs and FDs together create a framework — DPSPs direct the State to protect cultural diversity; FDs direct citizens to preserve it — forming a complementary constitutional protection of India's plural cultural heritage.

Value Addition:
• Article 29 protects 'any section of citizens' having a distinct language, script, or culture — it is broader than commonly understood and applies beyond religious minorities.
• The question of what counts as 'composite culture' is politically contested — majoritarian claims sometimes invoke 51A(f) against minority institutions.
• Article 30's protection for minority educational institutions has been expansively interpreted in T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002).

solution.concept_anchor: AIIMS Students Union — rights inherent, not earned through duties
solution.strong_distractor: b — ADM Jabalpur is strongly associated with the rights-duties discourse in Indian constitutional history — H.R. Khanna J.'s famous dissent touched on this very topic. Students may conflate Khanna J.'s dissent (which suggested duties-rights correlation) with the AIIMS ruling (which rejected duties as a condition for rights).
elimination_logic: The blank requires the case that explicitly held FDs are NOT a condition precedent to claiming FRs — a specific holding rejecting the correlation doctrine's strongest form.
Eliminate (a): Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic structure doctrine — it predates FDs and did not rule on the rights-duties correlation.

Eliminate (b): ADM Jabalpur (1976) is associated with H.R. Khanna J.'s dissent suggesting duties-rights correlation — but the majority held in favour of the State, not on duties as a condition for rights.
Eliminate (c): Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) expanded Article 21's scope — it did not address FDs as a condition precedent to rights.

Confirm (d): AIIMS Students Union v. AIIMS (2002) explicitly held that FDs are not a condition precedent to claiming FRs — rights are inherent attributes of citizenship, not earned through duty-performance.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes ADM Jabalpur for AIIMS Students Union. Both cases are associated with the rights-duties relationship: ADM Jabalpur contains H.R. Khanna J.'s famous dissent touching on citizens' duties to constitutional order; AIIMS Students Union explicitly rejected the correlation doctrine as a bar to FRs. A student who recalls 'duties-rights correlation + Supreme Court' will default to ADM Jabalpur without recognising that AIIMS Students Union is the case that definitively settled the specific question about FDs as a 'condition precedent.'
solution.final_explanation:
The question of whether failing to perform Fundamental Duties can forfeit one's Fundamental Rights was definitively answered by the Supreme Court.

• Option (a) — Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala: Incorrect. This 1973 case established the basic structure doctrine — it predates FDs (inserted in 1976) and did not address the rights-duties condition question.
• Option (b) — ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla: Incorrect. H.R. Khanna J.'s dissent in ADM Jabalpur did discuss the rights-duties nexus, but this was the minority view. The case itself was about whether courts could be approached during Emergency — not about FDs as conditions for rights.
• Option (c) — Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India: Incorrect. This 1978 landmark expanded Article 21 to include procedural fairness — it did not address the rights-duties correlation.
• Option (d) — AIIMS Students Union v. AIIMS (2002): Correct. The SC explicitly held that Fundamental Duties are not a condition precedent to claiming Fundamental Rights. Rights are inherent — they do not depend on prior performance of duties and cannot be forfeited by failing to perform them.

Value Addition:
• AIIMS Students Union v. AIIMS (2002) arose from a dispute about admissions — the Court's FD ruling was significant obiter dicta.
• This ruling protects citizens from 'authoritarian correlation' — the argument that dissidents who 'fail' their duty to the State lose their rights.
• The ruling aligns India with international human rights norms where rights are inherent and inalienable.

solution.concept_anchor: FDs apply to citizens only; FRs apply to persons including aliens

statement_analysis.statement: Fundamental Duties under Article 51A apply exclusively to citizens of India — non-citizens, including foreign nationals residing in India, owe no constitutional obligation under Part IV-A.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 51A is addressed to 'every citizen' — unlike some Fundamental Rights (such as those under Articles 14, 20, 21) which use the word 'person' or 'no person' and thus extend to non-citizens as well. FDs are citizen-specific obligations.

statement_analysis.statement: All Fundamental Rights under Part III of the Constitution apply equally to citizens and non-citizens — there is no Fundamental Right that is available only to citizens.
statement_analysis.reason: Several Fundamental Rights are available only to citizens: Article 15 (prohibition of discrimination on certain grounds), Article 16 (equality in public employment), Article 19 (freedom of speech, assembly, etc.), and Articles 29–30 (cultural and educational rights). Non-citizens cannot claim these rights.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who recall 'Article 14 says no person' and 'Article 21 protects all persons' may extrapolate this to all FRs and accept Statement 2 as true, without recalling that Articles 15, 16, 19, and 29–30 are citizen-specific.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: 'Every citizen' is the express language of Article 51A — non-citizens have no constitutional obligation under Part IV-A. Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: 'All Fundamental Rights apply equally to citizens and non-citizens' — Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, and 30 are citizen-specific. The claim that no FR is citizen-only is false. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Result: Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (b): Statement 1 is correct but Statement 2 is incorrect.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the scope-extension error. Students know that some important FRs (Articles 14, 20, 21) protect all 'persons' — and may generalise this to conclude that all FRs are universally applicable. The critical counter-examples are Articles 15, 16, 19, and 29–30, which use 'citizen' explicitly and are therefore available only to Indian citizens. This is a standard UPSC-pattern distinction — the split between 'person'-based and 'citizen'-based FRs is highly testable.
solution.final_explanation:
The citizenship dimension creates an asymmetry both within Fundamental Rights (some universal, some citizen-specific) and between FRs and FDs (FDs exclusively citizen-bound).

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 51A uses 'It shall be the duty of every citizen of India' — the express limitation to citizens means no foreign national residing in India bears any constitutional obligation under Part IV-A. This contrasts with FRs that apply to 'any person' (Articles 14, 20, 21).
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The claim that all FRs apply to citizens and non-citizens equally is false. Citizens-only FRs include: Article 15 (protection from discrimination), Article 16 (equal opportunity in public employment), Article 19 (six freedoms), Article 29 (cultural rights of any section of citizens), and Article 30 (minority educational institutions). Non-citizens can claim Articles 14, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, and 25–28 — but not all FRs.

Value Addition:
• The 'person vs. citizen' distinction in FRs is a standard UPSC distinction — memorise which rights use which term.
• Article 14 ('no person') — universally applicable. Article 19 ('all citizens') — citizens only.
• Corporations are 'persons' for Article 14 purposes — they cannot claim Article 19 freedoms (which are personal liberties).

solution.concept_anchor: Live constitutional tensions — 51A(h) vs. Article 25; 51A(e) vs. Article 19

statement_analysis.statement: No judicial decision has explicitly used Article 51A(h) — the duty to develop scientific temper — to strike down or override a practice protected under Article 25 on grounds of religious freedom.
statement_analysis.reason: Courts have carefully avoided a direct confrontation between 51A(h) and Article 25 — the tension between scientific temper and religious orthodoxy is a live constitutional issue without definitive judicial resolution.

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) held that Article 51A(e) — the duty to promote brotherhood — constitutes an independent head of restriction on freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a), separate from the grounds listed in Article 19(2).
statement_analysis.reason: Shreya Singhal held the opposite — restrictions on speech must find their basis in Article 19(2) grounds. FD 51A(e) is a supporting rationale, not an independent constitutional head for restricting speech. The Court struck down Section 66A IT Act despite claims based on protecting societal harmony.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(h) places a duty on citizens to develop scientific temper — but Article 25 extends its protection to 'all persons,' including non-citizens, while 51A(h) applies only to citizens, creating a scope asymmetry between the duty and the right it is said to be in tension with.
statement_analysis.reason: This is an accurate constitutional observation — 51A(h) applies to 'every citizen' while Article 25 protects 'all persons' including non-citizens. This citizenship-vs.-personhood asymmetry is a genuine constitutional nuance in the 51A(h) vs. Article 25 tension.

statement_analysis.statement: Maharashtra's Prevention and Eradication of Human Sacrifice and other Inhuman, Evil and Aghori Practices and Black Magic Act (2013) can be cited as a legislative measure that gives partial effect to Article 51A(h) by penalising practices inconsistent with scientific temper.
statement_analysis.reason: The Maharashtra anti-superstition law targets practices like human sacrifice, black magic, and exploitation through fraudulent supernatural claims — directly in the spirit of Article 51A(h)'s mandate for scientific temper, representing a legislative operationalization of this FD.

solution.strong_distractor: d — 'All four' is tempting because all four statements deal with real constitutional tensions and real laws — students who do not scrutinise Statement 2 carefully (which reverses the Shreya Singhal holding) may accept all four.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: No court has explicitly used 51A(h) to override Article 25 — this is accurate. Correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Shreya Singhal struck down Section 66A — it did not validate 51A(e) as an independent restriction ground. The statement reverses the holding. Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: 51A(h) = citizens; Article 25 = all persons — the scope asymmetry is a genuine constitutional observation. Correct.
Evaluate Statement 4: Maharashtra anti-superstition law does operationalize 51A(h) values. Correct. Three statements (1, 3, 4) correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the plausible-fabrication trap — it attributes to Shreya Singhal a holding that sounds judicially coherent ('51A(e) as independent head of restriction') but is precisely the opposite of what the Court held. Students familiar with Shreya Singhal as a speech-restriction case and with 51A(e) as having speech-restriction implications may accept the fabricated holding without recalling that the Court struck down Section 66A for failing Article 19(2) scrutiny, rejecting FD-based arguments as standalone grounds.
solution.final_explanation:
The live constitutional tensions between FDs and FRs reveal important structural features of India's constitutional design.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The courts' avoidance of a direct 51A(h) vs. Article 25 confrontation is deliberate judicial restraint — the political sensitivity of religion-science conflicts makes courts cautious.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Shreya Singhal explicitly rejected the idea that societal harmony (the theme of 51A(e)) can serve as an independent ground for speech restriction outside Article 19(2). Section 66A was struck down.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The citizenship-vs.-personhood asymmetry is constitutionally significant — 51A(h) applies to citizens; Article 25 protects all persons. This means the duty applies to a narrower set of persons than the right it is in tension with.
• Statement 4 — Correct: The Maharashtra anti-superstition law (2013) is a tangible legislative expression of Article 51A(h)'s aspiration — penalising exploitation through fraudulent supernatural practices and human sacrifice.

Value Addition:
• Narendra Dabholkar, anti-superstition activist, was instrumental in Maharashtra's 2013 law before his assassination.
• Karnataka and other states have considered similar legislation — 51A(h) provides the constitutional backing.
• Section 295A IPC (outraging religious feelings) and 51A(h) are in structural tension — courts have not resolved which prevails.

solution.concept_anchor: Negative fact — no duty to pay taxes in Article 51A
solution.strong_distractor: b — Paying taxes sounds like the most 'civic' obligation imaginable, and students who reason by analogy ('citizens have a duty to contribute to the State') will select this as if it were listed under Article 51A, confusing civic obligation with constitutional FD.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (b): Duty to pay taxes — Article 51A does not include this. Tax obligations arise from statutory law (Income Tax Act, GST), not from any Fundamental Duty.
Eliminate (c): Duty to vote in elections — Article 51A does not include this. Voting is a legal right and civic expectation, but not a constitutionally listed FD.
Eliminate (d): Duty to join the armed forces — Article 51A(d) only requires defending the country 'when called upon' — there is no compulsory military service duty listed as an absolute obligation.
Confirm (a): The duty to develop scientific temper, humanism, and spirit of inquiry and reform is expressly listed as Article 51A(h) — this is a correctly stated FD.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Options (b), (c), and (d) are plausible-fabrication distractors — each sounds like a legitimate citizen obligation in a democracy (paying taxes, voting, military service) but none is listed under Article 51A. The UPSC frequently tests negative facts about what FDs do NOT include. A student who reasons 'what should a responsible citizen do' rather than 'what does Article 51A specifically list' will be drawn to options (b) and (c). Only students who have memorised the precise list will correctly select (a).
solution.final_explanation:
Article 51A lists eleven specific Fundamental Duties — knowing what is NOT on the list is as important as knowing what is.

• Option (a) — Correct: Article 51A(h) expressly states the duty 'to develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform.' This is one of the more unique FDs — it is aspirational and values-based rather than action-specific.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: No duty to pay taxes appears in Article 51A. Tax payment is a statutory obligation under the Income Tax Act, GST statutes, etc. Tax evasion is a statutory offense — not a Fundamental Duty violation.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: No duty to vote is listed under Article 51A. Voting is a constitutional right (Article 326) and a civic expectation, but not a codified FD. Some countries mandate voting; India does not constitutionally require it.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Article 51A(d) creates a duty to defend the country and render national service 'when called upon' — but compulsory military service at all times is not an absolute FD. The duty is conditional ('when called upon').

Value Addition:
• The eleven FDs cover: constitutional respect, national struggle heritage, sovereignty, defence, national harmony, common brotherhood, composite culture, environment, scientific temper, excellence, and child education.
• 'When called upon' in 51A(d) is the trigger for military service duty — no standing conscription obligation exists.
• Goa is the only state with a uniform civil code — not a FD-derived outcome but a DPSP Article 44 aspiration.

solution.concept_anchor: 86th Amendment — Article 21A justiciable; 51A(k) non-justiciable; RTE implements 21A

statement_analysis.statement: The Right to Education Act, 2009, was enacted primarily to operationalize Article 51A(k) — the duty of parents to provide education — by penalising parents who fail to send their children to school.
statement_analysis.reason: The RTE Act 2009 was enacted primarily to operationalize Article 21A — the Fundamental Right to free and compulsory education. While it imposes obligations on parents (consistent with 51A(k)), its constitutional basis is Article 21A, not 51A(k).

statement_analysis.statement: Article 21A (Right to Education) and Article 51A(k) (duty of parent/guardian to provide education) were both inserted simultaneously by the same constitutional amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002, inserted both Article 21A and Article 51A(k) simultaneously — a unique co-creation of a Fundamental Right and a corresponding Fundamental Duty addressing the same age group (6–14 years).

statement_analysis.statement: A child between the ages of 6 and 14 years can approach a court to enforce the right to education under Article 21A — but the parent's duty under Article 51A(k) is not independently justiciable by the child.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 21A is a justiciable Fundamental Right — a child (through a guardian) can file a writ petition to enforce it. Article 51A(k) is non-justiciable; the child cannot independently invoke the parental duty as a basis for a court order against the parent.

solution.strong_distractor: a — '2 and 3 only' is tempting for students who correctly identify Statements 2 and 3 as accurate — but the strong distractor pressure is on students who accept Statement 1 as also true (thinking RTE implements parental duty, which it partly does, without recognising the constitutional basis distinction).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: RTE Act 2009 — primary constitutional basis is Article 21A (FR), not Article 51A(k) (FD). The statement incorrectly attributes the Act's primary basis. Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: 86th Amendment 2002 inserted both Article 21A and 51A(k) simultaneously — accurate. Correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: Article 21A is justiciable; 51A(k) is not independently justiciable by the child — accurately captures the asymmetry. Correct.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct — select option (d): '2 and 3 only.'
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the conflation between Article 21A and Article 51A(k) as the constitutional basis for the RTE Act. Both were inserted simultaneously, both address the 6–14 age group education, and the RTE Act does impose obligations on parents (consistent with 51A(k)). However, the RTE Act's primary constitutional basis is the Fundamental Right in Article 21A — not the non-justiciable FD in 51A(k). Students who know 'RTE + 51A(k) + same Amendment' may conflate the constitutional basis, selecting Statement 1 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
The 86th Amendment created a unique mirrored structure — a Fundamental Right (Article 21A) and a corresponding Fundamental Duty (Article 51A(k)) addressing the same subject.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The RTE Act 2009 was enacted to give effect to Article 21A — the Fundamental Right to free and compulsory education. Its primary constitutional mandate flows from Article 21A. While the Act imposes obligations on parents (resonating with 51A(k)), citing 51A(k) as the Act's primary constitutional basis is incorrect.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The 86th Amendment Act, 2002, is the unique constitutional amendment that simultaneously created both a new FR (Article 21A) and a new FD (Article 51A(k)) addressing the same age group — a deliberate co-creation reflecting the complementary rights-duties framework.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The asymmetry is fundamental — Article 21A creates a justiciable right that a child can enforce through a writ petition; Article 51A(k) creates a non-justiciable duty on parents that cannot be independently enforced by the child (though the State can enforce it through legislation).

Value Addition:
• The 86th Amendment also amended Article 45 (DPSP) — shifting the mandate from early childhood care (below 6) to the new 6–14 FR framework.
• RTE Act 2009 mandates 25% reservation in private unaided schools for EWS children — this provision was challenged and upheld in Society for Unaided Private Schools v. Union of India (2012).
• The RTE's implementation reveals how a Fundamental Right (21A) practically enforces the spirit of a non-justiciable FD (51A(k)) — an example of constitutional synergy.

solution.concept_anchor: BALCO principle — FDs cannot override economic policy; PIL limitation
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know 'PIL + FDs = courts can enforce environmental and social duties' may extrapolate to economic policy — selecting option (a) and assuming the Court would direct the State to abandon the privatization policy based on 51A(f) and related duties.
elimination_logic: The scenario involves privatization of a public sector entity — an economic policy decision by the executive and Parliament. The question is whether PIL citing FDs can override this.

Eliminate (a): PIL citing FDs (cultural heritage, livelihood) to compel reversal of privatisation policy — this is precisely what the SC cautioned against in BALCO. Courts cannot substitute economic judgment for executive judgment via FD-based PIL.

Eliminate (c): PIL is maintainable only against State action — private companies are not directly amenable to constitutional FD-based PIL. This option misstates the legal position by extending PIL to private actors in this context.
Eliminate (d): PIL courts do review the process of economic decisions but not substance in this manner — the statement misstates the scope of judicial review.

Confirm (b): BALCO Employees Union v. Union of India established that separation of powers prevents courts from using FDs to override economic policy decisions — PIL courts will not direct reversal of a privatization decision even if FDs are invoked.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap extends the logic of successful FD-based PIL (MC Mehta environmental cases) to economic policy — where the constitutional limit of judicial restraint is explicit. Students who know that PIL can enforce FDs in environment and social justice contexts may not recognise that economic policy is a distinct domain protected by the separation of powers, as articulated in BALCO. The key limiting principle: FDs can direct State action in favour of constitutional values, but cannot substitute judicial economic judgment for executive economic policy.
solution.final_explanation:
The BALCO principle is a critical judicial guardrail — it prevents FD-based PIL from becoming a mechanism for judicial second-guessing of economic policy.

In this scenario, the workers' union invokes FD 51A(f) (cultural heritage — public sector institutions as part of India's economic culture) and livelihood rights to reverse a privatisation decision.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: This is precisely what the SC rejected in BALCO Employees Union v. Union of India (2002). The Court held that privatization is a policy decision within the executive's domain — courts cannot use FDs to compel the State to abandon or reverse such decisions via PIL. Separation of powers is the limiting principle.
• Option (b) — Correct: Under BALCO, PIL courts will decline to direct reversal of privatisation on FD grounds. The Court will examine whether the process was constitutional (due process, non-arbitrariness) but will not substitute its economic judgment for the government's on the substance of privatisation.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: PIL maintainability is primarily against State action. While courts can regulate private polluters through FD-based PIL in environmental contexts, the privatisation decision itself is a State policy — the newly privatised entity's actions are a separate question.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Judicial review of economic decisions under Article 14 examines arbitrariness and reasonableness of the process — but FD 51A(f) does not transform livelihood concerns into an overriding constitutional ground against privatisation.

Value Addition:
• BALCO Employees Union v. UOI (2002) established the principle that economic policy decisions are not ordinarily subject to judicial review on FD grounds.
• The Court distinguished between 'manner of decision' (reviewable) and 'substantive decision to privatise' (not reviewable through PIL).
• This principle was reinforced in subsequent privatisation challenges — courts have consistently declined to reverse privatisation decisions using FD-based reasoning.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 23(2) — exception for compulsory public service; constitutional resolution

statement_analysis.statement: The constitutional tension between Article 23 (prohibition of forced labour) and Article 51A(d) (duty to defend the country) was left unresolved by the framers and has since been resolved through judicial interpretation alone.
statement_analysis.reason: The tension is constitutionally pre-resolved by Article 23(2), which explicitly exempts compulsory service for public purposes from the prohibition on forced labour. This was a deliberate textual resolution by the Constitution's framers, not a subsequent judicial innovation.

statement_analysis.statement: The USSR Constitution, which inspired the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation for FDs, treated rights and duties as co-equal and mutually reinforcing — with duties being equally enforceable alongside rights.
statement_analysis.reason: The Swaran Singh Committee explicitly drew from the Soviet constitutional model where rights and duties were co-equal and co-enforceable. India's adoption was softer — maintaining the rights-duties framework but keeping FDs non-justiciable.

statement_analysis.statement: The Agnipath military recruitment scheme launched in 2022 would be constitutionally vulnerable to challenge under Article 23's prohibition on forced labour if Parliament were to make participation compulsory, since no constitutional provision validates compulsory military service.
statement_analysis.reason: Compulsory military service, if enacted by Parliament, would be constitutionally valid under Article 23(2) — which exempts compulsory service for public purposes. Article 51A(d) provides additional support. Such legislation would not violate Article 23.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Statement 3 sounds plausible because Agnipath is a live controversy and students may not recall that Article 23(2) specifically validates compulsory public service, including military service, if Parliament enacts it.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The tension between Article 23 and 51A(d) is constitutionally pre-resolved by Article 23(2) — not left to judicial interpretation. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: The USSR constitutional model did treat rights and duties as co-equal and co-enforceable — the Swaran Singh Committee's explicit inspiration. Statement 2 IS correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: Article 23(2) explicitly validates compulsory public service; compulsory military service would not violate Article 23. Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses a live political controversy (Agnipath, 2022) to construct a plausible constitutional vulnerability claim. Students who know Article 23 prohibits forced labour and recall the Agnipath controversy may accept Statement 3 without recalling Article 23(2)'s explicit exception for compulsory public service. The temporal-swap element is also present — connecting a 2022 scheme to a constitutional provision without recalling the original exception built in by the framers in 1950.
solution.final_explanation:
The forced labour prohibition and the defence duty have a constitutionally elegant resolution — the framers built the answer directly into the text.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: Article 23(2) is the constitutional resolution — it explicitly carves out compulsory service for public purposes from the forced labour prohibition. This was not left for courts to resolve; the framers anticipated the need for national service and included the exception in the original Constitution (1950), predating both FDs (1976) and modern military debates.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Swaran Singh Committee's admiration for the Soviet model is well-documented. The USSR Constitution made duties co-enforceable with rights — a model India drew from while deliberately softening to non-justiciable FDs.
• Statement 3 — NOT correct: Compulsory military service legislation, if Parliament enacts it, would be constitutionally protected under Article 23(2). The only condition: it cannot discriminate on grounds of religion, race, caste, or class. Article 51A(d) provides further constitutional backing for such legislation.

Value Addition:
• Article 23(2) was a forward-looking provision — the framers anticipated the need for compulsory national service during national emergencies and defence needs.
• The Agnipath scheme is voluntary — but a compulsory version would be constitutionally valid under 23(2) + 51A(d).
• The Soviet model's collapse is often cited as evidence that making duties co-equal with rights in a coercive sense is constitutionally unsustainable.
